title: Exterior Painting Secrets Pro Crews Rarely Explain
description: Prep sequence, film thickness, dew point, and recoat timing decide whether exterior paint lasts. The details good crews follow and how to check for them.
excerpt: The prep order, weather rules, and film-thickness habits that separate an exterior paint job that lasts from one that peels early.
h1: Exterior Painting Secrets Professional Crews Do Not Advertise
heroIntro: Two houses can be painted the same color, with the same brand, in the same month, and look completely different three years later. The difference is almost never the label on the can. It is a handful of unglamorous habits.

sections.h2: Secret 1: the wall has to be clean, not just look clean
body: Most early paint failures trace back to what was on the wall when the paint went on. A layer of chalk from the old coating, a film of mildew, pollen, or road dust all sit between the new paint and the surface it is supposed to grip. The paint bonds to the contamination, and the contamination lets go.

Good crews start every exterior with a thorough wash and mildew treatment, then let the wall dry fully, often a full day or more in humid weather. A quick test tells you if a wall is ready: rub it with a dark cloth. If it comes away chalky, it is not ready. Our article on cleaning pollen off siding explains the low-pressure method that cleans without forcing water into the walls.

sections.h2: Secret 2: prep follows a strict order
body: Doing the right steps in the wrong order wastes them. The sequence that holds up looks like this:
bullets: Wash and treat mildew, then let the surface dry.
Scrape loose and peeling paint back to a sound edge.
Sand or feather the edges so they do not telegraph through the new coats.
Replace rotted wood and set or replace popped nails.
Spot-prime bare wood, bare masonry, and patches with the right primer for each.
Caulk joints and gaps after priming, since caulk sticks better to primed surfaces and primer will not cover fresh caulk well.
Protect landscaping, windows, fixtures, and hardscape before the first coat.

sections.h2: Secret 3: film thickness is the real warranty
body: Every paint has a recommended spread rate, the number of square feet a gallon should cover at a given thickness. Stretch it to cover more wall and the dried film ends up too thin to resist UV and moisture for long. A pro checks this with simple math (gallons used against area painted) and sometimes with a wet-film gauge. Two full coats at the specified thickness is the baseline, and dramatic color changes or porous surfaces like raw stucco often need a third.

Back-rolling or back-brushing sprayed paint is another quiet habit worth asking about. Spraying is fast and even, but on rough stucco and on wood it can bridge over pores and cracks. Rolling or brushing right behind the sprayer works the paint into the texture so it actually seals.

sections.h2: Secret 4: weather windows matter more than calendar dates
body: Paint needs the surface, not just the air, to be within the product’s temperature range, and it needs to stay above the dew point long enough to set. A common rule is to keep surface temperature at least 5°F above the dew point. In North Central Florida that is why summer work starts early and ends early: the morning gives the paint time to set before afternoon storms, and crews stop well before evening dew settles onto fresh film.

Direct sun is the other trap. A west wall in afternoon sun can be far hotter than the air temperature, which makes paint dry too fast to level and bond properly. Experienced crews follow the shade around the house. October through May is generally the most forgiving season for exterior work here; our guide to Florida weather and painting goes deeper into planning around it.

sections.h2: Secret 5: caulk is a system, not a cosmetic
body: Caulk is where many exterior jobs quietly fail. The wrong product shrinks, cracks, and lets water in behind fresh paint within a season. A durable exterior uses a high-performance sealant rated for the joint movement it will see, applied to clean, primed surfaces, tooled so it bonds to both sides of the gap. Deep gaps get backer rod first so the bead is the right shape and does not bond to the back of the joint, which would tear it as the wall moves.

Just as important is what does not get caulked. The bottom edges of lap siding, weep holes in windows, and the drip edges of sills are designed to let water out. Sealing them traps moisture inside the wall, and that trapped water shows up later as blistering and rot. A careful crew knows the difference.

sections.h2: Secret 6: the right product for each surface
body: A single product rarely suits a whole house. A strong, well-tested system usually looks something like this:
bullets: 100% acrylic on siding and trim for flexibility and UV resistance.
Elastomeric coating on stucco that has hairline movement, so it can stretch over small cracks.
A tougher enamel on doors, railings, and handled surfaces.
Penetrating stain, not paint, on exposed decks and some wood features that need to breathe.
Specialty primers for bare wood, tannin-bleeding woods, galvanized metal, and fresh masonry.

sections.h2: Secret 7: recoat windows and dry time
body: Each paint has a minimum time before it can be recoated and, for some products, a maximum time after which the next coat will not bond as well without scuffing. Rushing the second coat traps solvent and water in the first; waiting weeks between coats on some coatings lets dust, pollen, and chalk build up in between. Good crews plan the day around these windows, and they leave adequate cure time before re-hanging shutters or closing doors against fresh paint.

sections.h2: How to check for these habits when you hire
body: Ask any contractor to show you, in writing, what prep is included, which primer and topcoat products they will use, how many coats, and how they handle weather delays. Vague answers like "we’ll wash it and paint it" are a red flag. If you manage an association, our HOA guide to hiring licensed, insured painters adds the paperwork side.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year to paint a house exterior in Florida?
faqs.a: October through May is generally the most forgiving window in North Central Florida. Summer work is possible but should start early in the day and stop before afternoon storms and evening dew.

faqs.q: Why does exterior paint peel after only a year or two?
faqs.a: Usually because it was applied over chalk, mildew, dirt, or a damp surface, or applied too thin. The paint bonds to the contamination instead of the wall and lets go.

faqs.q: Is spraying exterior paint as good as rolling?
faqs.a: Spraying is efficient and even, but on stucco and wood it should be back-rolled or back-brushed so the paint penetrates the texture and seals pores and small gaps.

faqs.q: Do I need primer when repainting the exterior?
faqs.a: Sound, clean, previously painted surfaces may not need full priming, but any bare wood, bare masonry, patches, or stained areas should be spot-primed with the correct primer.
